checks.invariant: gitleaks runs in the hunt only as `dir|git <one literal path inside the project>` with a redaction flag, a JSON report written only under reviews/<id>/, and no flag that reads stdin, a baseline, an ignore file, a template, a diagnostics folder or follows symlinks
checks.result: huntGitleaks (:900-958) walks every word through huntOptions (:652-678), which refuses a null word, `--`, an `=`-attached form of a plain flag and any flag not on the spec. A verb other than dir/git/version/help is refused, as is a third positional or a missing path. --report-format/-f must equal json, --log-opts must match the alnum-led `a..b` regex, so no option can be injected into git log. The scan path goes through literalPathWhy and then checkProjectDir (caller :2132), which resolves symlinks and 8.3 names and refuses a path outside the project. --config must be a literal path inside the project. Each --report-path goes through checkTarget (:2131), which holds it to reviews/<id>/ and .ultrapowers/ and keeps the run records protected. No redaction-free form is reachable: `--redact=0`, `--redact=abc`, `--redact false` and an absent flag are all refused. The only gap is that --redact=1..99 is accepted (partial redaction, hardening below); I found no way to print or record a secret value with a form the allow-list accepts that the agent could not already get from a recursive grep or git show.

checks.invariant: gitleaks cannot be started through a package runner or a wrapper in a form the redaction rule never judged
checks.result: The viaRunner refusal (qa-shell-writes.mjs:696) names HUNT_AUDIT_TOOLS, which now includes gitleaks (:609). env/timeout/command/xargs wrappers are walked and re-dispatched to the same huntCheck call, so the redaction rule applies to them. The bash layer (qa-guardrail:1166-1168) runs the same analyzer and fails closed when it cannot run. The one path that skips the form is a path-qualified program name, because huntCheck sees only the basename; that is the candidate recorded under the hunt allow-list unit, not a gitleaks-specific flaw.

checks.invariant: isKeyMaterial is the same key list as the hook's file-tool rule, and its move out of qa-shell-writes.mjs changed no behaviour
checks.result: git diff dev..GH-63-cloudflare-engine shows the KEY_RE removed from qa-shell-writes.mjs and added to guard-paths.mjs byte for byte, with every caller switched to isKeyMaterial (:1356, :1532, :1536, :1575, :2287), so the move is behaviour-neutral. The list is not the same as the file-tool rule in hooks/qa-guardrail:637, although the comment at guard-paths.mjs:177 claims it is: the file-tool regex denies the whole `.aws/` folder, the shell version only `.aws/credentials`. A read of `~/.aws/cli/cache/*.json` or `~/.aws/sso/cache/*.json` (cached temporary credentials and SSO bearer tokens) is therefore denied through the Read tool and allowed through `cat` (candidate hunt-guardrail/key-material-aws-cache-weaker-in-shell-rule). The 8.3 and symlink resolution in checkAlias (:1559-1576) is correct for in-project words, but a `~` word is judged by text only (`plain` is false).

checks.invariant: a key-material path field or glob in any hunt tool call is denied before the hunt's tool gate and the write rules
checks.result: The node block collects every path-shaped field and glob field (:471-490), and the bash block denies a KEY_RE match on the typed and the real spelling (:647-664) and on a glob that can expand to a key name (:666), before the hunt gate (:767) and the file-tool gate (:873). `.env.example` is stripped deliberately. A tool with an unreadable path or a twotargets call is denied (:550, :589-593). No bypass found for the tools the hunt gate lets through.

checks.invariant: every program a hunt shell command starts is on the allow-list, and a program named by a path inside the project is refused (huntProgramWhy :1165-1177)
checks.result: The path-named-program refusal lives only in huntProgramWhy (:1169-1177). simple() takes progName(args[0].v), which is the basename (:72, :1725), calls huntCheck (:2128) and returns at :2130-2133 when huntCheck allows, before huntProgramWhy runs at :2139. Every program huntCheck allows is therefore started under whatever path the agent wrote: date, npm, pnpm, pip, dotnet, cargo, pip-audit, osv-scanner, and in this range gitleaks (:609, :889). No test covers a path-qualified audit tool (tests/qa-gatekeeper has no such case). Recorded as a candidate: hunt-guardrail/audit-form-skips-program-path-check.

checks.invariant: the plugin's own scripts the hunt may run with node (HUNT_OWN_SCRIPTS_RE, extended in this range with hunt-sandbox, hunt-verdict and the two validators) are the plugin's files, not the audited tree's
checks.result: huntProgramWhy (:1233-1256) requires the script to be the first word after node with no option, free of `..`, not stdin, matching the anchored regex on the real path, outside the report area, inside the real plugin root, and a regular file. The env gate (:2112-2116) refuses NODE_OPTIONS and the other loader variables before it. The arguments of these scripts are not judged by the guardrail, only by name for key material. The validators (validate-findings.cjs, validate-coverage-ledger.cjs) take one path, read it, and write nothing. The same-checkout case (plugin root equal to the audited project) trusts the audited tree by construction and is not a boundary here.

checks.invariant: a tool the hunt does not use, a tool that carries a URL, and a tracker or mail tool that writes are all denied in the hunt profile
checks.result: The hunt gate (:767-799) denies web fetch and search names, any non-reader tool with a URL, the write_stdin forms, and any tool not on hunt_write_re, hunt_shell_re or hunt_tools_re unless its MCP server is a tracker or mail word, so unknown MCP tools and other connectors (Drive, Calendar, Firecrawl, Canva) are denied. Tracker and mail tools pass as reads. The write-vs-read decision for them (:705-731) is a verb list in which `trash`, `mark`, `archive`, `request` and `apply` are missing, so Gmail trash_message, trash_thread, mark_message_spam and mark_thread_spam, and GitHub request_copilot_review, are classified as reads and pass (candidate hunt-guardrail/tracker-write-verb-denylist-misses-trash-mark).

candidates.title: A path-named program runs on the host when its basename is an allowed hunt audit form
candidates.description: The hunt guardrail judges the program by its basename. When the basename and arguments match an allowed audit form (date, npm audit, pip list, cargo audit, osv-scanner, pip-audit, and in this range gitleaks), the call is allowed and the rule that refuses a program named by a path inside the project is never run. A hunter steered by repository text can then run an executable file of the audited tree, or on Windows Git Bash a `#!` script it wrote into reviews/<id>/, under a name such as `./gitleaks` or `reviews/<id>/date`, directly on the host with the developer's credentials. This is outside the Docker sandbox, which AGENTS.md and the hunt contract make the only door to project code. A sibling control (`bash reviews/x.sh` is refused) shows the intent.
candidates.claimed_root_cause: In simple(), huntCheck is called with the basename-only prog and returns at `if (h && h.allow) { ...; return; }` before huntProgramWhy, which is the only place that refuses a path-named program inside the project.

trace.description: The program word, which may be a path such as ./gitleaks or reviews/<id>/date, becomes prog = progName(args[0].v).
progName keeps only the basename, lowercased, without .exe, so the directory part of the path is dropped.
gitleaks (and date at 798, osv-scanner at 874, the package managers) are judged by their arguments only and return allow() with no look at the path.
The refusal of a program that is a path inside the project exists only here, and it is reached only for programs huntCheck did not allow.
`if (h && h.allow) { ... return; }` ends the check, so the call passes and the shell starts the file at the given path.

evidence.description: huntCheck receives prog (the basename) and the argument values, never the original program word.
huntProgramWhy is called after the huntCheck return, so an allowed audit form never reaches it.
gitleaks was added to HUNT_AUDIT_TOOLS in this range (diff dev..GH-63-cloudflare-engine); the huntCheck-before-huntProgramWhy order itself is unchanged and already existed for the other tools.
The bash layer adds no executable-path rule for the hunt; it only runs the same analyzer (:1166).

blockers: No sandbox for this run, so the analyzer cannot be executed to observe the allow decision

Whether an executable named like an allowed tool exists in the audited tree (Linux), or whether MSYS runs a `#!` file written into reviews/<id>/ without an exec bit (Windows), is a deployment fact outside source

validation_plan.local: In a throwaway project with a hunt run record, feed hooks/qa-guardrail the PreToolUse event {tool_name: Bash, command: `./bin/gitleaks --version`} and then `reviews/<id>/date +%s` with a harmless shebang file there. Expect the analyzer to refuse a path-named program, as it does for `bash repo/script.sh`; an allow, or a run of the file, confirms the candidate.
validation_plan.deployment: Owner check: on the machine that runs hunts, create reviews/<id>/gitleaks as a one-line `#!/bin/sh` script that only prints a marker, and see whether a hunter session is allowed to run `reviews/<id>/gitleaks --version`.

candidates.title: The shell key-material rule lets a hunter read ~/.aws/cli/cache and ~/.aws/sso/cache that the file-tool rule denies
candidates.description: The file-tool rule in hooks/qa-guardrail denies the whole `.aws/` folder. The shell rule isKeyMaterial (guard-paths.mjs) names only `.aws/credentials`, and the bash text rule at :1143 does the same. The hunt allows cat, head, grep and similar on paths outside the project, so a prompt-injected hunter can read the AWS CLI's cached role credentials and SSO access tokens through the shell and put them in its context or in a committed reviews/<id>/ file, while the Read tool refuses the same file.
candidates.claimed_root_cause: Two copies of the key list disagree: the file-tool KEY_RE uses `(^|/)\.aws(/|$)` and the shared isKeyMaterial uses `\.aws\/credentials`, although the comment on isKeyMaterial says it is the same list as the hook's shell rule.

trace.description: A shell word such as ~/.aws/cli/cache/token.json is judged by text only, because a `~` word is not 'plain' (:1561).
isKeyMaterial(keyText(word)) is the only key-name test for the word.
The shell copy of the key list matches `.aws/credentials` but not `.aws/cli/cache/*` or `.aws/sso/cache/*`.
cat, head, tail and grep are on the hunt's program list and read any path, so the file is printed.

evidence.description: The file-tool KEY_RE denies `(^|/)\.aws(/|$)`, so the Read tool refuses the same file the shell reads.
The bash text rule over the command also names only `.aws/credentials`.
The comment claims the list is the same as the hook's shell rule; the two regexes differ.
keyGlobReaches (guard-paths.mjs:121) lists only .aws/credentials among the AWS names, so a glob such as ~/.aws/cli/cache/*.json is not caught either.

blockers: No sandbox for this run, so the analyzer was not executed on `cat ~/.aws/sso/cache/x.json`
Whether the developer's machine holds a populated ~/.aws/cli/cache or ~/.aws/sso/cache is a deployment fact

validation_plan.local: In a throwaway project with a hunt run record, feed hooks/qa-guardrail `cat ~/.aws/sso/cache/a.json` through Bash and `~/.aws/sso/cache/a.json` through Read, and compare: the shell call is expected to be allowed and the Read call denied.
validation_plan.deployment: Owner check: list ~/.aws/cli/cache and ~/.aws/sso/cache on the hunting machine to see whether live credentials sit there; if so, align both lists on the whole `.aws/` folder.

candidates.title: The hunt lets mail and tracker tools with the verbs trash, mark, archive or request through as reads
candidates.description: A hunt may call MCP tools of a tracker or mail server, and the hook tells a write from a read by a list of write words. The list has no `trash`, `mark`, `archive`, `request` or `apply`, so Gmail trash_message, trash_thread, mark_message_spam and mark_thread_spam (and their untrash/unmark pairs) and GitHub request_copilot_review are not recognised as writes and pass the hunt gate. Repository text that steers a hunter could trash or spam-mark the developer's mail or trigger a review request, in a run that is meant to read and never post.
candidates.claimed_root_cause: The tracker/mail read-write decision (qa-guardrail:709-731) is a denylist of write verbs and passes any name that holds none of them; the hunt gate (:796-799) then treats every tracker-word server as a reader.

trace.description: A tool such as mcp__claude_ai_Gmail__trash_message is normalised and matches tracker_re (gmail).
write_re lists create, update, delete, label, send, post and similar words, but not trash, mark, archive, request or apply, and read_re does not match either.
The deny fires only when write_re matches and read_re does not; a name matching neither falls through.
The tracker server word sets tracker_read=1, so the hunt gate at :797 does not deny the tool.
The call is allowed and the MCP server moves the message to Trash or marks it as spam.

evidence.description: The deny message states the intent: tracker and mail writes through MCP tools are never run during a hunt; the run reads, it does not post.
The hunt's tracker word list includes gmail, outlook, slack and teams besides the code trackers.

blockers: No sandbox for this run, so the hook was not executed on these tool names
Whether a Gmail, Slack or other mail/chat connector with such tool names is loaded and authorised in the session that runs a hunt is a harness and deployment fact

validation_plan.local: Feed hooks/qa-guardrail, under a hunt run record in a throwaway project, the events {tool_name: mcp__claude_ai_Gmail__trash_message, tool_input: {}} and {tool_name: mcp__claude_ai_Gmail__mark_thread_spam, tool_input: {}}; both are expected to be allowed, while mcp__claude_ai_Gmail__create_draft is denied.
validation_plan.deployment: Owner check: see whether the harness used for hunts exposes a mail or chat connector with trash, mark or archive tools; if it does, add those verbs (or switch to a read-verb allow-list) for the tracker rule.

hardening: huntGitleaks accepts --redact=1..99 (qa-shell-writes.mjs:913). Per gitleaks' documented semantics a partial percent leaves (100-n)% of the secret visible, while hunt-verdict.mjs:246-252 treats only Secret '' or 'REDACTED' as redacted. Accept only bare --redact or --redact=100. It adds no capability beyond recursive grep today, because the key rule is name-based, so this is hardening.

huntGitleaks allows --log-level trace|debug and -v/--verbose (:899, :918). Whether gitleaks logs raw secret text at those levels with --redact is a gitleaks behaviour I could not observe; limit --log-level to info and above.

The key-material rule is name-based: a recursive grep -r or rg --hidden over the project, and gitleaks dir over it, read an in-tree .env without naming it (the /proc recursion check at qa-shell-writes.mjs:2726 is the only recursion rule).

The key list lacks .dev.vars (the project's own Claude settings deny it), .envrc, id_dsa, ~/.m2/settings.xml, ~/.gradle/gradle.properties, ~/.terraform.d/credentials.tfrc.json and ~/.config/pip; the shell, file-tool and bash-text copies (guard-paths.mjs:180, qa-guardrail:637, :1143) should be generated from one list.

The arguments of HUNT_OWN_SCRIPTS_RE scripts are not judged by the guardrail. hunt-verdict.mjs `validate` reads any path the agent names (key names are denied by word only), and its error output echoes validator or JSON parse text.

The tracker rule treats a name with any read word (get, list, search, resolve) as a read even when it also holds a write verb (a name such as get_or_create_x); a read-verb allow-list for tracker tools is stronger than the write denylist.

uncovered.surface: skills/vulnerability-hunt/prompts/lane-secrets.md step 1 passes the audited tree's .gitleaks.toml as --config
uncovered.boundary: audited-branch configuration controls what the secrets lane can detect
uncovered.reason: The guardrail accepts any --config inside the project (qa-shell-writes.mjs:948), and gitleaks also auto-loads .gitleaks.toml from the scanned path. A branch under audit can allowlist its own committed secrets and the lane reports 'ok, none'. This is a prompt and contract question (h5 owns the prompts) with a preflight side, not a guardrail rule.

uncovered.boundary: front-page writes reviews/<id>/SECURITY-REPORT.md under the root found from --cwd, which the guardrail does not judge
uncovered.reason: Because the guardrail lets hunt-verdict.mjs run with unjudged arguments, `front-page <id> --cwd <other project>` can overwrite an existing SECURITY-REPORT.md in another ultrapowers project (hunt-verdict.mjs:749-788). The unit is h4's (loadRun/verdict/front-page) and needs its own deterministic coverage.
